claims: Stiff-Person Syndrome (SPS) is a rare, chronic autoimmune neurological disorder.
SPS is characterized by progressive muscle rigidity, stiffness, and painful spasms.
SPS spasms are often triggered by noise, touch, or stress.
SPS affects twice as many women as men.
SPS typically causes severe mobility issues including difficulty walking.
No cure exists for SPS.
Treatments like sedatives and immunotherapy help manage symptoms of SPS.
Symptoms of SPS often begin in the 30s-40s.
Symptoms of SPS progress slowly.
Severe stiffness in the trunk, spine, and limbs (especially legs) occurs in SPS.
Severe stiffness in SPS often leads to a board-like appearance.
Intense often unpredictable muscle spasms occur in SPS.
Muscle spasms in SPS can cause falls, injuries, and in some cases broken bones.
Lumbar hyperlordosis (an arched back) develops in SPS.
Difficulty walking leading to a stiff-legged gait occurs in SPS.
Extreme sensitivity to external stimuli including sound, touch, and cold occurs in SPS.
Sensitivity to external stimuli can trigger spasms in SPS.
High anxiety often linked to the fear of falling or having a spasm in public occurs in SPS.
Many SPS patients have high levels of anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) antibodies.
Anti-GAD antibodies inhibit the neurotransmitter responsible for relaxing muscles.
SPS often coexists with other autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, thyroiditis, vitiligo, and anemia.
In some cases SPS acts as a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with breast, lung, or colon cancers.
SPS is often misdiagnosed initially due to its rarity.
Blood tests for anti-GAD antibodies confirm SPS diagnosis.
Electromyography (EMG) detects electrical activity in muscles to confirm SPS diagnosis.
Clinical observation of symptoms confirms SPS diagnosis.
If left untreated SPS can progress to severe disability.
With proper treatment many individuals with SPS can manage symptoms.
Individuals with SPS often require long-term care.
Muscle relaxants such as diazepam or Valium manage spasms and rigidity in SPS.
Sedatives manage spasms and rigidity in SPS.
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) modulates the immune system in SPS treatment.
Plasmapheresis modulates the immune system in SPS treatment.
Physical therapies help manage movement and function in SPS.
Aquatic therapies help manage movement and function in SPS.
